entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes

Title: General QC Processes
Subtitle: Field reminders for key quality processes used on site.
Process cards: 01 Inspection Planning: Prepare the inspection so the right work is checked against the right requirements at the right time.
02 Requirement Review: Establish what 'acceptable' means before inspecting or making a quality decision.
03 ITP / PIE / PRIE Execution: Use the approved inspection/test plan to control inspection sequence, responsibilities, intervention points and records.
04 Hold & Witness Points: Control critical inspection stages so required parties can verify work before it proceeds.
05 Inspection & Acceptance: Verify completed or in-progress work against defined requirements and record an objective result.
06 Deficiency Reporting: Record an observed quality issue that requires correction but is handled below the project's formal NCR threshold.
07 Non-Conformity Reporting (NCR): Control, document and resolve work, material or installation that does not conform to an applicable requirement.
08 Corrective Action: Implement and verify action that removes the cause or condition associated with a quality problem and prevents or reduces recurrence where required.
09 Reinspection & Verification: Confirm that corrected, repaired, reworked or otherwise dispositioned work now satisfies the required condition.
10 Quality Evidence & Photo Documentation: Create objective, retrievable evidence that shows what was inspected, where, when and against what requirement.
11 Testing & Test Records: Plan, witness, record and evaluate required quality tests using approved methods and traceable results.
12 Material Receiving & Verification: Verify delivered materials/equipment are correct, approved, undamaged and traceable before incorporation into the work.
13 RFI / Technical Clarification: Obtain an authorized clarification when contract information is missing, conflicting, ambiguous or unsuitable for a reliable field decision.
14 Change & Revised Document Control: Ensure field decisions and inspections use the latest authorized information and that changes remain traceable.
15 Traceability: Maintain a defensible chain connecting the installed work to requirements, materials, inspections, tests, issues, approvals and closeout records.
16 Quality Closeout: Confirm required quality obligations are complete, verified, organized and ready for turnover.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Inspection Planning

Summary: Prepare the inspection so the right work is checked against the right requirements at the right time.
When to Use: Before planned work, before a defined inspection point, or whenever upcoming work may become concealed or difficult to verify later.
Field Workflow: 1. Define the inspection scope: Identify the activity, location, lot/area and stage of work to be inspected.
2. Review requirements: Check current drawings, specifications, approved submittals, ITP/PIE/PRIE, procedures and applicable acceptance criteria.
3. Identify inspection points: Confirm hold, witness, surveillance and testing points and required notifications.
4. Confirm prerequisites: Verify preceding work, approvals, materials, access, equipment and test readiness.
5. Coordinate timing: Align with superintendent/foreman, subcontractor, testing agency and owner/consultant as required.
6. Prepare tools and records: Have checklist, measuring tools, camera, drawings and forms ready.
7. Inspect before concealment: Arrive early enough to observe the condition before it is covered or altered.
Key Reminders: Plan from the work sequence, not only from the calendar.
A good inspection starts before arriving at the workface.
If a critical point may be missed, communicate early.
Common Mistakes: Inspecting after concealment
Using an old drawing revision
Arriving without knowing acceptance criteria
Failing to coordinate third-party or owner witness requirements

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Requirement Review

Summary: Establish what 'acceptable' means before inspecting or making a quality decision.
When to Use: Before inspection, testing, acceptance, deficiency/NCR issuance, material verification, or whenever requirements appear conflicting or unclear.
Field Workflow: 1. Identify the work: Define the exact component, system, location and activity.
2. Find governing documents: Locate contract drawings/specifications and applicable approved procedures.
3. Confirm current revision: Verify the document is approved/current for construction.
4. Check supporting requirements: Review approved submittals, shop drawings, RFIs, changes, manufacturer instructions and ITP criteria.
5. Resolve conflicts: Do not invent an interpretation; identify discrepancies and obtain clarification through the approved channel.
6. Extract acceptance criteria: Convert the requirement into observable or measurable checks.
7. Record the basis: Keep the document/revision reference supporting the inspection decision.
Key Reminders: Verify the requirement first; do not inspect from memory when the requirement is available.
A manufacturer instruction does not automatically override the contract hierarchy.
If documents conflict, escalate through the project's defined authority chain.
Common Mistakes: Judging from personal preference
Using superseded drawings
Quoting a requirement without its revision/context
Treating an unresolved conflict as a field decision
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → ITP / PIE / PRIE Execution

Summary: Use the approved inspection/test plan to control inspection sequence, responsibilities, intervention points and records.
When to Use: When an activity is governed by an ITP, PIE, PRIE or equivalent inspection/testing plan.
Field Workflow: 1. Select the applicable plan: Confirm activity, scope and revision.
2. Review sequence and responsibilities: Know who performs, verifies, witnesses and accepts each point.
3. Confirm prerequisites: Ensure preceding stages and required approvals are complete.
4. Respect intervention points: Do not pass a hold point without required release; provide witness notice as required.
5. Perform/observe checks: Complete inspections and tests against listed criteria.
6. Record results: Enter objective results, references, evidence and signatures/approvals as required.
7. Address failures: Route deficiencies or non-conformities through the defined process.
8. Complete the record: Ensure all required stages are signed/closed and traceable.
What to Capture: Linked test reports, photos, NCRs or deficiencies
Key Reminders: The ITP is a control map, not merely a form to sign at the end.
A missed hold point can invalidate downstream assurance.
Use the project's definitions for H/W/S/R points.
Common Mistakes: Back-filling signatures
Skipping points because the work looks acceptable
Treating witness and hold points as interchangeable
Failing to link supporting records
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Hold & Witness Points

Summary: Control critical inspection stages so required parties can verify work before it proceeds.
When to Use: When the ITP/quality plan or contract defines hold, witness, review or surveillance points.
Field Workflow: 1. Identify the point: Confirm type, requirement, responsible party and notification period.
2. Verify readiness: Ensure work and prerequisite documentation are ready for inspection.
3. Notify required parties: Issue notice using the approved communication method and lead time.
4. Maintain control: For a hold point, do not proceed until formal release is obtained.
5. Perform/observe inspection: Record observations, results and evidence.
6. Obtain disposition/release: Capture required acceptance, waiver or authorized release.
7. Record traceability: Link the release to the activity, location and inspection record.
Key Reminders: Hold point = stop until authorized release, unless the governing procedure expressly provides otherwise.
Witness-point rules can vary; follow the project's notification and waiver procedure.
Never self-release a point outside your authority.
Common Mistakes: Proceeding because the inspector did not arrive
Verbal release with no record when formal release is required
Late notification
Confusing surveillance with hold/witness requirements
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Inspection & Acceptance

Summary: Verify completed or in-progress work against defined requirements and record an objective result.
When to Use: At planned inspection stages, before concealment, at completion of an activity, or when acceptance is required.
Field Workflow: 1. Confirm inspection basis: Verify scope, location and current requirements.
2. Observe the work: Inspect condition, installation, workmanship and interfaces.
3. Measure/test as required: Use suitable calibrated/verified tools where measurement is required.
4. Compare with criteria: Determine compliance against explicit requirements.
5. Record evidence: Capture results, measurements, photos and references.
6. Classify result: Accept, identify deficiency, initiate NCR, or seek clarification according to project rules.
7. Communicate result: Notify responsible parties and record required approvals.
8. Preserve traceability: Link the inspection to location, activity and supporting records.
Key Reminders: Acceptance must be based on requirements, not appearance alone.
Record actual values when a measurable criterion exists.
Do not sign for work you did not inspect unless the procedure explicitly permits record-based verification.
Common Mistakes: 'Looks good' without criteria
Recording only pass/fail with no evidence for critical checks
Accepting concealed work that was not verified
Using uncalibrated equipment where calibration is required
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Deficiency Reporting

Summary: Record an observed quality issue that requires correction but is handled below the project's formal NCR threshold.
When to Use: When work has a correctable issue and the project quality plan permits it to be managed as a deficiency/punch item rather than an NCR.
Field Workflow: 1. Identify the issue: State what is wrong and where.
2. Verify the requirement: Confirm the expected condition.
3. Document evidence: Capture objective description, location and photos/measurements.
4. Classify correctly: Confirm the issue belongs in the deficiency process rather than NCR or RFI.
5. Notify responsible party: Assign/communicate through the approved process.
6. Correct the work: Responsible party completes correction.
7. Reinspect: Verify the corrected condition.
8. Close: Record verification and closure evidence.
Key Reminders: A deficiency is not a way to avoid an NCR when the NCR criteria are met.
Describe the condition, not the person who caused it.
Closure requires verification.
Common Mistakes: Vague descriptions such as 'fix wall'
No location reference
Closing from a contractor's message without verification
Using deficiency and NCR terminology interchangeably
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Non-Conformity Reporting (NCR)

Summary: Control, document and resolve work, material or installation that does not conform to an applicable requirement.
When to Use: When the project's NCR criteria are met: a specified requirement is not satisfied and formal control/disposition is required.
Field Workflow: 1. Identify the non-conformity: Determine exactly what does not comply and where.
2. Verify the requirement: Confirm the applicable drawing, specification, approved submittal, procedure, code or other governing requirement.
3. Control the condition: Prevent concealment, continuation, use or incorporation of affected work where required.
4. Document objective evidence: Record location, element ID, condition, photos, measurements and requirement.
5. Notify responsible parties: Follow the project's NCR communication and quality procedure.
6. Determine disposition: Use authorized disposition such as rework, repair, replace, reject, or accept-as-is/concession where formally permitted.
7. Implement corrective action: Ensure the approved disposition/action is completed.
8. Reinspect / verify: Confirm the resulting work satisfies the approved disposition and applicable requirements.
9. Close and retain traceability: Record verification, evidence, approvals and formal closure.
Key Reminders: Do not close the NCR merely because the repair was performed; verify the completed work first.
Do not prescribe an engineering disposition unless you have the authority to do so.
Keep the original non-conforming condition traceable to its final disposition.
If accept-as-is/use-as-is is proposed, obtain the approval required by the contract and quality procedure.
Common Mistakes: Writing the NCR before confirming the requirement
Blaming individuals instead of describing facts
Allowing affected work to be concealed
Using 'repair' and 'rework' casually where the project distinguishes them
Closing without disposition approval or verification
Additional Sections: Project-specific variation: Terminology, disposition authority, stop-work/containment requirements and NCR thresholds vary by organization and contract. Follow the approved project quality plan.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Corrective Action

Summary: Implement and verify action that removes the cause or condition associated with a quality problem and prevents or reduces recurrence where required.
When to Use: When an NCR, repeated deficiency, audit finding, trend, test failure or other quality event requires formal corrective action.
Field Workflow: 1. Define the problem: State the issue and scope using evidence.
2. Contain immediate risk: Control affected work/material where necessary.
3. Determine cause: Use an appropriate root-cause method proportional to significance.
4. Define action: Specify what will correct the condition and, where required, address recurrence.
5. Assign responsibility and due date: Make ownership and timing explicit.
6. Implement action: Complete approved actions and retain evidence.
7. Verify effectiveness: Check that the action worked, not merely that it was performed.
8. Close: Document verification and approval.
Key Reminders: Correction fixes a detected condition; corrective action may address why it occurred. Follow project terminology.
Root-cause depth should match risk/significance.
Effectiveness verification may require observing later work, not only reviewing a completed form.
Common Mistakes: Calling every repair a root-cause corrective action
Choosing a cause without evidence
Closing immediately after implementation
Actions with no owner or due date
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Reinspection & Verification

Summary: Confirm that corrected, repaired, reworked or otherwise dispositioned work now satisfies the required condition.
When to Use: After deficiency correction, NCR disposition, failed inspection/test, or corrective work requiring verification.
Field Workflow: 1. Review original issue: Understand the requirement, condition and approved disposition.
2. Confirm correction is complete: Ensure the work is ready for verification.
3. Inspect the affected work: Verify the correction itself and relevant interfaces.
4. Repeat measurements/tests where required: Use the same acceptance basis or approved revised basis.
5. Compare with requirements: Determine whether closure criteria are met.
6. Record evidence: Capture results, photos, measurements and linked records.
7. Close or return: Close only if acceptable; otherwise keep open/escalate.
Key Reminders: Reinspection is an independent verification step, not an administrative checkbox.
Verify the whole affected condition where the correction could create secondary issues.
Maintain linkage to the original record.
Common Mistakes: Checking only that work was attempted
Closing without viewing inaccessible corrected work
Creating a new unrelated record with no link to the original
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Quality Evidence & Photo Documentation

Summary: Create objective, retrievable evidence that shows what was inspected, where, when and against what requirement.
When to Use: During inspections, tests, receiving, deficiencies/NCRs, corrective work, concealed-work verification and closeout.
Field Workflow: 1. Define what must be proven: Know the condition/result the evidence needs to support.
2. Capture context: Take an overview establishing location/orientation.
3. Capture detail: Photograph the specific feature, defect, measurement or identification.
4. Include scale/ID where useful: Use measuring device, tag, gridline or element identifier without obscuring the condition.
5. Record metadata: Link date, location, activity and record ID.
6. Add concise notes: Describe what the image demonstrates.
7. Store and link: Place evidence in the approved system and connect it to the relevant record.
Key Reminders: A photo without context may prove very little.
Capture evidence before concealment or correction when possible.
Do not rely on photos alone when a measurement/test record is required.
Follow project privacy/security rules when people, sensitive assets or restricted information may appear.
Common Mistakes: Only close-up photos with no location context
Blurry or dark images
No caption or record linkage
Photographing a tape measure at an unreadable angle
Using edited images that obscure original evidence
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Testing & Test Records

Summary: Plan, witness, record and evaluate required quality tests using approved methods and traceable results.
When to Use: When specifications, codes, ITPs or procedures require testing of materials, systems or completed work.
Field Workflow: 1. Confirm test requirement: Identify method, frequency, sample/location and acceptance criteria.
2. Verify readiness: Confirm test area/material, equipment and prerequisites.
3. Verify test resources: Check qualified personnel/laboratory and calibration/certification where required.
4. Identify sample/test: Assign traceable sample, location or equipment identification.
5. Perform or witness test: Follow approved method and record actual results.
6. Evaluate result: Compare against acceptance criteria.
7. Control failures: Notify and initiate required deficiency/NCR/retest process.
8. File final record: Link signed report and supporting evidence to the work.
Key Reminders: Record actual test values, not just 'pass'.
A retest does not erase the original failed result.
Confirm sampling frequency and location requirements before work advances.
Common Mistakes: Missing sample location
No calibration traceability
Discarding failed results after a passing retest
Using wrong units or acceptance criteria
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Material Receiving & Verification

Summary: Verify delivered materials/equipment are correct, approved, undamaged and traceable before incorporation into the work.
When to Use: At delivery, before storage/use, and before installation where receiving verification is required.
Field Workflow: 1. Identify delivery: Confirm purchase/submittal/material description and intended use.
2. Verify approval status: Check approved submittal/product data and required certifications.
3. Inspect condition: Look for damage, contamination, deterioration or improper packaging.
4. Verify identification: Check manufacturer, model/type, grade, size, heat/batch/lot numbers where applicable.
5. Review documentation: Confirm delivery ticket, certificates, test reports and compliance documents.
6. Check storage requirements: Protect material from damage or environmental exposure.
7. Accept, quarantine or reject: Apply project controls to nonconforming or unverified material.
8. Record traceability: Link material to delivery, lot and installation area where required.
Key Reminders: Approved product does not mean every delivered unit is automatically acceptable.
Preserve identification needed for later traceability.
Quarantine unverified/nonconforming material according to project procedure.
Common Mistakes: Material installed before approval
Certificates filed without linking them to delivered lots
Damaged material accepted because product type is correct
Losing batch/heat identification
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → RFI / Technical Clarification

Summary: Obtain an authorized clarification when contract information is missing, conflicting, ambiguous or unsuitable for a reliable field decision.
When to Use: When the inspector cannot determine the requirement without interpretation or when documents conflict.
Field Workflow: 1. Define the question: State the exact technical issue and location.
2. Research existing information: Check drawings, specifications, submittals, prior RFIs and changes first.
3. Describe the conflict/gap: Reference the affected documents and revisions.
4. State field impact: Identify work affected, timing or quality risk without overstating.
5. Submit through approved channel: Use the project's RFI/clarification process.
6. Track response: Do not treat informal discussion as final where formal response is required.
7. Verify implementation: Ensure the authorized response is reflected in the work and records.
8. Link downstream records: Connect response to inspection/change/as-built documentation.
Key Reminders: Ask a focused question; do not write an RFI that hides the actual conflict.
An RFI is not automatically authorization to change scope, cost or design.
Use the response only within the authority and scope stated.
Common Mistakes: Submitting before checking available documents
Suggesting an unapproved design solution as if accepted
Proceeding on a verbal answer when formal response is required
Failing to link the response to affected inspections
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Change & Revised Document Control

Summary: Ensure field decisions and inspections use the latest authorized information and that changes remain traceable.
When to Use: When drawings, specifications, RFIs, site instructions, change notices, shop drawings or procedures are revised.
Field Workflow: 1. Receive authorized revision: Confirm source, status and approval.
2. Identify affected work: Determine systems, locations, inspections and records impacted.
3. Withdraw superseded information: Prevent unintended field use according to document-control procedure.
4. Distribute current information: Ensure relevant teams have access.
5. Review quality impact: Update inspection criteria, ITPs/checklists or pending inspections where needed.
6. Verify field implementation: Check work reflects the authorized revision.
7. Preserve revision history: Maintain traceability between old/new documents and affected records.
Key Reminders: 'Latest file received' is not always 'approved for construction.' Verify status.
Never erase revision history needed to explain earlier inspections.
Revisit completed or ongoing work if a revision has retrospective impact.
Common Mistakes: Inspecting from a superseded drawing
Deleting old records rather than superseding them
Assuming an RFI response is a formal drawing revision
No impact review for work already installed
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Traceability

Summary: Maintain a defensible chain connecting the installed work to requirements, materials, inspections, tests, issues, approvals and closeout records.
When to Use: Throughout construction, especially for critical materials, concealed work, testing, NCRs and turnover documentation.
Field Workflow: 1. Define traceability requirement: Know what identifiers and links the project requires.
2. Assign/use stable identifiers: Use location, lot, batch, heat, serial, inspection or record IDs.
3. Link source records: Connect materials, certificates, submittals and requirements.
4. Link execution records: Connect inspections, tests, photos and ITP points.
5. Link issues and dispositions: Maintain NCR/deficiency/corrective-action linkage.
6. Preserve revisions: Keep the document basis used at the time of inspection.
7. Verify completeness: Check the chain can be followed without relying on memory.
8. Transfer to closeout: Organize records for turnover/retention.
Key Reminders: A record is traceable only if another person can follow the chain later.
Use consistent identifiers across systems.
Do not depend on filenames alone where metadata/record IDs are available.
Common Mistakes: Photos not linked to an activity
Certificates with no installed-location linkage
NCR closure detached from original inspection
Renaming files in ways that break references
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Quality Closeout

Summary: Confirm required quality obligations are complete, verified, organized and ready for turnover.
When to Use: At system, area, milestone or project completion and before final quality turnover.
Field Workflow: 1. Define closeout requirements: Review contract, quality plan and turnover checklist.
2. Check inspections/tests: Confirm required records are complete and accepted.
3. Resolve open issues: Close or formally disposition deficiencies, NCRs and corrective actions.
4. Verify final condition: Complete final inspections/punch verification as required.
5. Assemble records: Organize ITPs, inspection reports, test reports, certificates, approvals and evidence.
6. Check traceability: Confirm records can be linked to systems/areas/assets.
7. Verify document status: Ensure final/as-built/O&M/commissioning interfaces are coordinated where within QC scope.
8. Complete turnover: Obtain required reviews, approvals and retention/hand-off.
Key Reminders: Closeout begins during construction, not at the end.
Do not hide unresolved items to make the dossier appear complete.
Verify completeness and retrievability, not merely file count.
Common Mistakes: Waiting until project end to organize records
Missing signatures/revisions
Open NCRs buried in turnover files
Duplicate/uncontrolled records with unclear final status
Additional Sections: No additional source-backed sections are displayed.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → General QC Processes → Universal Field Reference

Before Any Inspection: Confirm the exact work and location.
Confirm current approved drawings/specifications and applicable submittals.
Know the acceptance criteria and tolerances.
Check ITP/PIE/PRIE points, notifications and prerequisites.
Have suitable measuring/test tools and required forms.
When You Find a Problem: Do not jump immediately to an NCR: first verify the requirement and project classification rules.
Record the actual condition objectively and precisely.
Use the approved communication and escalation path.
Do not design the fix unless that authority is part of your role.
Verify the completed correction/disposition before closure.
Minimum Useful Quality Record: Observation/result: What did I actually see or measure?
Decision/status: Accepted, deficient, NCR, clarification, pending?
Responsibility: Who must act or approve?
Follow-up: What happens next and by when?
Closure: Who verified it, when, and against what basis?
Important Limitation: This guide provides generic field reminders. Contract documents, codes, approved project procedures, owner requirements, delegated authority and the project quality plan govern.
Terminology such as deficiency, NCR, observation, punch item, repair, rework, concession, hold point and witness point may be defined differently by different projects.
Where safety, structural integrity, life-safety systems or engineering acceptance is implicated, follow the project's escalation and professional-responsibility requirements.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Systems → 01 Sitework & Earthworks → 1.1 Existing Conditions

Summary / Objective:
This workflow establishes what existed before CRT's work affected the area.
That sounds mundane, but it protects the project against disputes and prevents existing utilities/services/structures from being inadvertently damaged.
The four main subjects are:

Before considering a structural zone complete
A structural element is not “quality complete” merely because it is physically standing.
correct requirement + approved material + correct installation + required inspection/testing + objective evidence + resolved deviations + verified closure
Absolutely. Building envelope deserves one of the deepest modules in the whole system because envelope defects are often:
difficult to diagnose once the building is closed;
directly tied to water infiltration, air leakage, condensation, heat loss, mold, corrosion, and occupant complaints.

Create a continuous, durable, coordinated environmental separation between exterior and interior conditions, with controlled water, air, vapour and heat flow across walls, openings, penetrations and transitions.
And the key word is continuity.
A wall can have excellent insulation, excellent membrane, excellent flashing, and still fail if those systems are not properly connected at:
windows → doors → roof → foundation → penetrations → corners → joints → structural interfaces.
So our envelope QC system must inspect not only components, but also interfaces.

PRACTICAL EXAMPLE — FLOOR FINISH IN AN ELECTRICAL ROOM
Suppose epoxy floor coating is scheduled tomorrow.
You should not simply arrive when they're already rolling coating.
Finishes → Concrete Floor PreparationthenFinishes → Floor Finishes → Epoxy/Coatings
If substrate fails, coating doesn't start.
Because an otherwise perfect epoxy floor can be destroyed by another trade dragging equipment across it before cure.
That last step—protection of accepted finished work—is particularly important in this phase.

Evidence & Documentation: PRACTICAL EXAMPLE — PIPE ABOVE A FIRE-RATED CEILING
Suppose a mechanical contractor finishes piping above a ceiling and the architectural trade wants to close the ceiling tomorrow.
You do not merely inspect the pipe.
Mechanical → piping systemMechanical → penetrationsMechanical → testingMechanical → insulationInterior Architectural → ceilingsFire/Life Safety → firestopping
Photograph the entire hidden system before ceiling closure.
Now, if there is ever a future dispute, you have evidence of what existed before concealment.
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE — HVAC UNIT ARRIVES ON SITE

Approved equipment?→ Receiving damage?→ Correct tag/model?→ Correct base/curb?→ Correct orientation?→ Maintenance clearance?→ Anchorage?→ Vibration isolation?→ Duct/piping/drain connections?→ Electrical/controls interfaces?→ Start-up?→ Commissioning?
That is how the system prevents you from thinking
“Equipment is sitting there, therefore installation is good.”

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Gates → Envelope Pre-Concealment Gate

Summary / Purpose: Ensure building-envelope control layers and interfaces are acceptable before subsequent layers make them inaccessible.
Prerequisites: Substrate is acceptable, dry and clean where required, and repaired.
Control layers use the correct product and are continuous, with seams, laps, and transitions complete.
Openings and penetrations have coordinated transitions, restored membranes, restored insulation continuity, flashing, and seals.
Concealed interfaces are photographed and deficiencies are corrected.
Blocking Conditions: Tear or discontinuity in air/water control layer, unsealed penetration, wet or damaged insulation, incomplete window/door transition, incomplete flashing, or unresolved envelope deficiency about to be concealed.
Release Condition: Envelope layer ready for covering or the next assembly layer in the affected scope.
Release Information: Conditional hard means hard only when the envelope condition applies. This guide does not create contractual release authority.
Gate Tip: Gates define universal quality logic. They are not live project approvals, signatures, or release records.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Gates → Underground / Pre-Backfill Gate

Summary / Purpose: Prevent burial of underground work until the service, geometry, tests, traceability, and required release conditions are complete for the affected segment.
Prerequisites: Route, trench/subgrade, service type, material, size, elevation, slope, joints, crossings, separations, structures, testing, as-built survey, photos, and service identification are complete.
Blocking Conditions: Failed or missing test, wrong elevation or slope, unaccepted joint/connection, missing as-built capture, open deficiency about to be buried, or missing required release.
Release Condition: Ready for backfill for the affected underground segment.
Release Information: This guide gate does not create an official backfill release; governing project requirements control actual release.
Gate Tip: Gates define universal quality logic. They are not live project approvals, signatures, or release records.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Gates → External Works Completion Gate

Prerequisites: Below-grade utilities, testing, as-builts, structures, backfill, compaction, base/subbase, drainage, surfaces, transitions, restoration, fencing where applicable, cleanup, and issue closure are complete.
Release Condition: External works quality complete for final closeout guidance.
Release Information: This is final external-work guide readiness, not official owner or client acceptance.
Gate Tip: Gates define universal quality logic. They are not live project approvals, signatures, or release records.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Gates → Final Turnover / Acceptance Gate

Summary / Purpose: Determine whether physical work, quality issues, testing, records, and owner-readiness requirements have converged sufficiently for turnover guidance.
Prerequisites: Physical work, quality issue closure, testing, commissioning, records, owner readiness, specialist/professional acceptance where required, quality package, and turnover package are complete under governing requirements.
Blocking Conditions: Significant/open deficiency, open NCR, missing or failed test, incomplete commissioning, missing acceptance evidence, missing required as-built/O&M/certificate/warranty, incomplete owner-readiness deliverable, or incomplete formal acceptance dependency.
Release Condition: Ready for turnover/acceptance guidance when governing project requirements and authorized acceptance dependencies are satisfied for the scope.
Release Information: This guide gate is not a formal turnover approval, client acceptance, signature, release, or official project status.
Gate Tip: Gates define universal quality logic. They are not live project approvals, signatures, or release records.

entries.breadcrumb: Home → Gates → Interior Wall / Ceiling Pre-Concealment Gate

Summary / Purpose: Prevent wall or ceiling closure until concealed architectural, MEP, fire/acoustic, and access conditions are acceptable.

Fire, acoustic, damper, valve, junction-box, and access requirements have been addressed with evidence captured.

Release Condition: Wall or ceiling ready to close for the affected area.
Release Information: This is a closure-readiness guide gate only. It is not an official project release, approval, or inspection record.
